articles.title: Ukraine's path to EU accession narrows as war drags on
Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough
articles.summary: Talks in Abu Dhabi centred around Europe's security framework, with US envoys due to meet Putin and Zelensky on Thursday.
articles.body: On Thursday Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will travel to Moscow and Dublin to hold talks with the Russian and Ukrainian presidents Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day. Although the American side said they saw "some openings", there was no hint of any breakthroughs to end the nearly five year-long war sparked by Russia's invasion. However, both Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange was in the works and could be carried out soon. Davyd Arakhamia from Ukraine's negotiating team said that this round of talks - the first since February - "was one of the hardest." "I believe the Russians came with very strict directives, so it was extremely difficult to soften the discussion," he said. But he added that he felt "good momentum" and urged for a second round of talks to be organised as soon as possible. Comments by Kremlin negotiator Vladimir Medinsky were less conciliatory. "Right now... a lot depends on Ukraine, on the position of the US, and on whether Europe comes to its senses," he said. After the talks it was announced that on Thursday US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner - President Donald Trump's son-in-law - would travel to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, and then to Dublin to speak to Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky. The meetings in Abu Dhabi had been framed as centred around the "security architecture" of Europe. For Kyiv, this may include reassurances that allies will come to its aid if Ukraine comes under attack again, despite the country not being a Nato member. For Moscow, a reworked "security framework" is likely to include a limit to the influence of Nato in eastern Europe - a central concern for the Kremlin since the alliance's eastward expansion. Earlier this week Kushner said the US hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that could "secure lasting peace", while the Kremlin's Medinsky said the world needed a "new" and "fair" security system. That framework would serve as "a new Yalta and Potsdam", Medinsky said, referring to the 1940s summits in which the victorious Allied powers carved up post-war Europe into spheres of influence. Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin. Representatives of Britain, Nato and various EU countries were also in Abu Dhabi and met with US and Ukrainian negotiators, but the Kremlin - with whom the EU does not officially communicate - said its delegation had not had any contact with them. Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent. Many - particularly in eastern Europe - feel their security is linked to that of Ukraine. Agreements cannot be implemented "if no consensus can be reached among Nato members," a German government spokesperson said on Wednesday. Kushner said the US was keen to bring the Europeans on board and said that getting them "added to the format" would be on the agenda for his talks with Putin. There is also disagreement on whether discussions on a future security framework should be preceded by a ceasefire, as the Europeans and Kyiv would want, or whether the fighting only stops after an agreement has been reached, as the Kremlin has insisted. Any agreement on a peacetime security framework, however, is contingent on the war ending, Kushner noted. But that cannot occur "until there's an agreement on territory and on all other bilateral issues," he added. Since talks began last year, a core obstacle to any settlement has been Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia. Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas, which it says are essential to its security. Moscow, meanwhile, has never backed down from its demand that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds. "Every inch" of land would be "returned to Russia one way or another", Medinsky said. Kushner acknowledged that the territorial question remained the hardest, while Zelensky's chief of staff and negotiator Kyrylo Budanov refused to be drawn on whether Russia was still demanding a Ukrainian withdrawal from the region. Later, Budanov admitted the talks had been "tough" and that Ukraine's priority was to ensure Russia could not attack it again. "These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex," Kushner said. "The reality is there is no trust right now between the sides and that is to be expected after a conflict like this." Inside devastated front-line city that Russia wants Ukraine to give up

articles.title: Daily Life In A Belarus Women's Prison, As Lukashenko Mulls Amnesty
articles.summary: As the authorities in Minsk consider an amnesty for women behind bars, RFE/RL's Belarus Service has spoken to two former political prisoners about the daily reality of being incarcerated.
articles.body: At 6 a.m. every day a message blasts through a Soviet-era loudspeaker and the lights switch on, jolting from their sleep 20-40 women in bunk beds in a cell at Prison Number 4 in Homel, southeastern Belarus. It's one of two women's prisons in the country that may soon experience a reduction in inmates amid planned legislation for an amnesty with a special focus on women. It's not yet known how many prisoners will benefit. Several thousand women are currently locked up, including 111 who are defined by exiled human rights group Vyasna as political prisoners. In Homel, women convicted on political charges must sleep on the top bunk and must wear yellow tags to identify their status. Two such women were human rights campaigner Nasta Loyka and civic activist Palina Sharenda-Panasyuk , who described daily life in jail to RFE/RL's Belarus Service . Both served time in Homel, while Sharenda-Panasyuk was also held in Zarechcha, some 100 kilometers to the west. It is a former military facility housing repeat offenders with 70-100 women in each room. Belarus Holding At Least 22 Political Prisoners In Psychiatric Hospitals, Rights Groups Say Vyasna figures currently classify 91 women in Homel as political prisoners, and just one in Zarechcha. After being woken up, the inmates must get ready. Loyka said that in one section 100 women shared seven washbasins and four toilets. "In 20 minutes, 100 people must make their bed in a special-shaped ‘envelope,' get dressed, take their pajamas to the locker room, go to the toilet, brush their teeth, and comb their hair," she said. By 6.15-6.20 a.m., the women are lining up for a breakfast of porridge, white bread, and tea. Those who come last get about 10 minutes to eat. Work begins at 8 a.m., but before that the women must line up for inspection in the yard. Those with yellow tags stand in the front rows. In Homel, this gives them a brief glimpse of the outside world as apartment blocks can be seen above several rings of prison fences. "We see the windows of these homes. When it's New Year's Day, a holiday, people hang up a lot of garlands, hearts, stars. We see something so beautiful," Loyka said. There are then random searches before they enter the factory. "When you unbutton your jacket, they check your pockets and grope you completely," Loyka said. 'Worms Instead Of Meat': Female Ex-Political Prisoners Describe Belarus's 'Nightmare' Penal System Most women work at a garment factory. Women cut, sew, and iron uniforms. A place in the cutting shop is one of the most highly paid jobs, earning more than 100 rubles a month (roughly $30). For women who are forbidden to transfer money from home, such as those on the official "terrorist list," this is a relief. Around 3 p.m., the first shift leaves the shops and the second shifts come in. Lunch is at noon and lasts about an hour. At Zarechcha, the work is similar, but here the women sew uniforms for the Russian Army and Belarusian security forces. Sharenda-Panasyuk said that in her experience other convicts treated political prisoners better at Zarechcha, warning them of snitches and trying not to provoke them. Sharenda-Panasyuk recalled that in Zarechcha prisoners were fed cold meat three times. When asked whether that meant three times a week or a month, she answered, "Three times a year." Sometimes the women sorted through rotten onions, carrots, beets, and cabbage to seek vitamins not on the prison diet. "They would just take this beet or carrot; it's all in the ground. They'd wipe it on the stove, which is almost never washed, and scrape something off. And then they eat these dirty vegetables. They peel the onion and eat it, too," she said. After work, inmates have some free time to read or write letters. In Homel, it's compulsory to watch "educational broadcasts" on state TV. At 4 p.m., the second of the day's inspections takes place and at 8 p.m. a third, exclusively for those with yellow tags. There's also a library, a gym, a church, and a club where events and concerts are held. But often these are inaccessible to political prisoners. "The day we go to wash is automatically a little more pleasant," said Loyka. Other high points include a weekly shopping day and calls to relatives three times a month. Long meetings with loved ones (from one to three days) are allowed three times a year. However, any of these privileges can be revoked for violations. Those deemed to be breaking prison rules can also be sent to a punishment cell: a cold, concrete room. Violations can include such trivial actions as hugging someone, borrowing toilet paper, leaving the top button of their dress undone, or talking during an inspection. Loyka said the objectification and abuse of women by male guards was also an issue. Sometimes, the men would watch the inmates on surveillance cameras. "When we'd come back in the evening, the women would change. One employee would not only watch (on a monitor), he would also comment if someone had holes in her underwear.... Some male employees would come in (on the pretense of) checking the sinks or even the toilets," she said. Loyka added that one officer repeatedly said the inmates' mandatory breast badges were crooked and would rip them off their uniforms. Sharenda-Panasyuk described harsh work conditions in Zarechcha that included being harnessed to a cart like a horse and pulling heavy loads. She said political prisoners were put under extra pressure by being housed in units with mentally ill inmates who could turn violent. At 9.30 p.m., inmates can go to bed. At 10 p.m., workers from the second shift return to their cells. Sharenda-Panasyuk described a frantic rush to be first to arrive back, get access to a washbasin, and have time to drink tea. "It looks a little comical, but behind this comedy lies a great human tragedy," she said. Once everyone is in bed, there is neither total darkness nor any sense of calm: Prison guards roam the rooms throughout the night, shining their flashlights. RFE/RL's Belarus Service is one of the leading providers of news and analysis to Belarusian audiences in their own language. It is a bulwark against pervasive Russian propaganda and defies the government’s virtual monopoly on domestic broadcast media.

Spain sees widespread disruption in first general strike for 14 years
articles.summary: Protests are also expected in the biggest cities less than three weeks before Spaniards vote in parliamentary elections.
articles.body: Watch: Protesters gather across Spain for first general strike in 14 years Transport and other public services across Spain have faced serious disruption in the first general strike for 14 years called by the main unions over housing and the high cost of living. Demonstrations have taken place across the country, including in Madrid and Barcelona, where tens of thousands marched in the evening. The head of the big UGT labour union, Pepe Álvarez, said the strike was a success with "massive" participation, while Unai Sordo of the CC OO union said turnout was "very significant." However, the Spanish Confederation of Business Organisations said participation was "low and uneven", depending on the areas and sectors involved. The general strike took place little more than two weeks ahead of national elections in Spain Some of the biggest disruption on Wednesday was seen in the main industrial hubs of Madrid and the north-eastern region of Catalonia where traffic was halted on several main roads. The interior ministry said dozens of people were arrested for a variety of incidents and Spanish reports said estate agencies had seen attacks on their offices. The strike was triggered by widespread protests over affordable housing and rising living costs, after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from a flat in Madrid where she had lived for seven decades. She died in hospital weeks later. Rental prices in the capital have soared in recent years. The monthly cost of a 50m sq apartment in Madrid was an average of €1,170 in October, according to property portal Idealista, while Spain's average gross monthly salary is about €2,460 (£2,056). That amounts to nearly half the average gross salary, well above the 30% level of affordability often recommended by housing experts and public institutions. Tyres were set on fire in the city of Gijon in northern Spain Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called snap elections last month after parliament failed to approve his plan for housing reform. Not since 2012, under the conservative government of Mariano Rajoy, has Spain held general strikes. And while previous strikes have been problematic for the government in power, this one is different. Sánchez and his ministers have even encouraged workers to down tools and demand affordable housing. "Your eight-hour day. Your pension. Your public healthcare… These were collective conquests," he wrote on social media, praising those who took part in previous strikes. Dramatic eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage The conservative People's Party (PP), by contrast, has accused the government of attempting to weaponise the strike for electoral gain. PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo called the general strike "nonsense", calling the unions "mafia" and "trash". Feijoo's party is leading in the polls and party spokesman Miguel Tellado accused the government of exploiting the strike to warn voters against allowing a right-wing government to be formed, which looks the most likely outcome of the 29 November election. Sánchez told Spanish TV this week: "What is nonsense is to question the rights of workers to strike." Gonzalo Álvarez, who was taking part in the general strike, says 50% of his salary goes towards rent Among those taking part in the general strike was Gonzalo Álvarez, 27, who was visiting different picket lines in central Madrid. Although he works in sales, he has been volunteering for a housing union that tries to protect tenants and makes them aware of their rights. The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal at the end of September "was the little fire" that sparked this protest, he told the BBC. Álvarez knew the 87-year-old, who had faced a tripling of her rent under new landlords, and says he was deeply upset by her treatment. He rents a small, one-bedroom flat with his girlfriend, a dental hygienist, in the city's southern Arganzuela disrict. The couple pay €1,000 between them, which means each spends about half of their salary on housing, even before other bills. He sees no way of getting on the property ladder: "You have to collect an insane amount of money to be able to buy a house. So with these salaries, it's impossible." With current rent and purchase prices, he believes buying somewhere is "completely impossible". However, the vice-president of the CEOE, Spanish biggest business association, Miguel Garrido, criticised the strike, complaining that businesses had little to do with the price of housing. "This is not a strike for labour-related reasons, but rather for political ones, and it is closely linked to the early calling of elections," he said. Demonstrations were planned for some of Spain's biggest cities later in the day and the scale of support will be widely viewed as an indicator of public discontent ahead of the election. Another reliable indicator of support for strikes is the level of demand for electricity with Spain's industrial sector. Power usage in Spain fell by 7.5% during the early hours of Wednesday, according to data from operator Red Eléctrica. During the last general strike 14 years ago, equivalent consumption was down by more than 15%.

articles.title: Spain: Housing crisis prompts general strike
articles.summary: Workers across nearly all industries have taken to the picket lines as rents soar and the housing crunch worsens. The crisis is the main political debate ahead of Spain's November 29 elections.
articles.body: Workers across Spain gathered en mass on Wednesday, marching and setting up picket lines despite stormy weather in many areas of the country. This is the first general strike in Spain in 14 years, amid a worsening cost of living and lack of housing crisis that has left many unable to support themselves. Symbolized by the eviction and death of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal in Madrid earlier this year, the crisis has also prompted a snap election set for November 29. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The government of left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez attempted to pass legislation to ease the plight of renters, but was blocked in parliament by opposition parties. Lacking the power to get legislation passed, Sanchez called the early vote in hopes to shore up more support. Sanchez's government did end up approving two extraordinary decrees introducing measures similar to the housing reforms rejected by parliament. "We won't stop until we transform this country's housing model from top to bottom so that houses are for living instead of being at the service of the [landlord] minority," said Alicia del Rio, spokesperson for the Madrid Tenants' Union. While most of the protests appeared to be proceeding peacefully, strikers in front of Madrid's Mercamadrid wholesale market said that police had used pepper spray on the crowd, prompting at least 13 people to seek medical attention. Some airlines later reported disruptions on flights in and out of Spain as some airport and airline workers participated in the strike. The country has a deficit of about 750,000 homes, which is set ​to grow to more than a million by 2028 according to estimates from the central bank. With fewer and fewer individuals and families able to buy a home, the number of renters in the country has risen sharply. According to Spain's youth council, the average rent is €1,176 ($1,315). This is equivalent to 99% of the average young person's salary. The general strike comes a day after rail workers launched a strike over two major deadly train crashes this year, making decrepit infrastructure also a major topic in the upcoming parliamentary elections. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The government has support the strike, saying it is being held "in favor of rights" rather than against anyone. Sources close to Sanchez inner circle have gone so far as to say it is "against the opposition." Alberto Nunez Feijoo, leader of the conservative People’s Party (PP), stated that if this is indeed "a strike against the opposition," it is "an absurdity the likes of which does not exist in any other European Union country." Although the UGT labor union, one of the organizers of the strike, and Sanchez's socialist PSOE party are two separate institutions, they do share a historic founder in Pablo Iglesias Posse. Nicole Ris, reporting for DW in Madrid, has been following the strike closely as it unfolds on Wednesday. Here's what she has to say: Here in Madrid apparently lots of people are still showing up for work and people I know have clearly said they will not go on strike as they don't see much sense in it (although they all suffer under the cost living crisis and the housing crisis). "I'm not taking part in this. It's nonsense. The government is supporting it because they hope they'll get enough votes on the 29th so they can carry on," a doorman in Madrid told me. There is also a debate about this strike being an "election strike" that could benefit the current government. The government supports the strike, claiming it is being held "in favor of rights" rather than against anyone. Sources close to Sanchez's inner circle have gone so far as to say it is "against the opposition," according to the media here.

articles.title: Kidnapper, 74, escapes from house arrest in Argentina by abseiling from balcony
articles.summary: Leonardo Bertulazzi, a former member of the Marxist guerrilla group the Red Brigades, was about to be extradited to his home country of Italy.
articles.body: Leonardo Bertulazzi was first arrested in Buenos Aires in 2002 A 74-year-old Italian man who was found guilty of a kidnapping carried out by a far-left militant group in the 1970s has escaped while under house arrest in Argentina and is on the run. Leonardo Bertulazzi used a harness to abseil down from a fifth-floor balcony in the capital, Buenos Aires. His escape was not immediately registered because he had tampered with his electronic ankle monitor so that it continued to transmit body temperature measurements even after he had prised it open and absconded. Bertulazzi already spent decades as a fugitive after he was sentenced in absentia in Italy for the 1977 kidnapping of Italian naval engineer Pietro Costa. He was awaiting extradition to Italy and was being monitored by the Argentine ministry of security through an ankle tag which registers the wearer's body temperature and movements. Officials said that they had become suspicious when they noticed that the tag had remained stationary. When they entered the fifth-floor apartment in the centre of Buenos Aires, Bertulazzi was gone, but the ankle monitor remained. Wary of Bertulazzi's past with the Marxist guerilla group the Red Brigades and his bomb-making skills, police called in explosives experts in case it had been rigged to detonate, according to Argentine newspaper Clarín. However, the experts found that while Bertulazzi had tampered with the device, he had done so to prevent the alarm from sounding once he removed it. Italian media say that his extradition to Italy had been imminent after his last appeal was rejected. Bertulazzi was first arrested after using a false passport to cross into Argentina from neighbouring Chile in 2002. However, he was granted refugee status in 2004 and lived freely in the South American country until his re-arrest in 2024, when the current right-wing president, Javier Milei, took office. Milei's government said at the time that "Bertulazzi is responsible for crimes that undermined democratic values and the lives of many victims". He was a member of the Red Brigades, which kidnapped and killed a number of state officials in the 1970s and '80s. Bertulazzi was part of the Red Brigades' Genoa section that kidnapped Pietro Costa on the street and then held him for 81 days before receiving a big ransom. The money it made from the kidnapping was then used to buy a flat in Rome, which was used in 1978 for the Red Brigades' most notorious crime, the kidnap and murder of Italian former Prime Minister, Aldo Moro. Moro was abducted when his car was ambushed on the way to the opening of parliament. He was held in the flat for 54 days before he was shot and his body abandoned in the boot of a Renault car in the centre of Rome.

Gorduladze: Opposition trying to turn Constitutional Court proceedings into TV debates and a show
articles.summary: Archil Gordulაძე, Chairman of the Parliament's Legal Affairs Committee, has accused opposition representatives of attempting to turn the ongoing Constitutional Court proceedings into television debates and a show. Commenting on today's hearing, Gorduladze said representatives of what he described as unconstitutional parties were continuing their efforts to undermine the legal process through what he called demagoguery.
articles.body: Archil Gordulაძე, Chairman of the Parliament's Legal Affairs Committee, has accused opposition representatives of attempting to turn the ongoing Constitutional Court proceedings into television debates and a show. Commenting on today's hearing, Gorduladze said representatives of what he described as unconstitutional parties were continuing their efforts to undermine the legal process through what he called demagoguery. “They know that their unconstitutional actions have no legal justification, and now they are trying to get by solely through demagoguery,” Gorduladze said. He also criticized what he described as legally absurd demands, citing Nika Gvaramia's call for the Constitutional Court to adopt part of its final decision on the same day. “Such a thing has never been attempted, not only in the history of the Constitutional Court, but also in the history of the common courts and Georgian justice,” he said. Gorduladze added that when opposition parties lack legal grounds for their arguments, they resort either to legal nonsense as a lifeline or to what he described as actions dictated by those giving them instructions. Related story: Constitutional Court issues official statement on lawsuit seeking to ban five political parties

articles.title: Several fires detected at Ust-Luga port after drone attack: "Novatek" facility ablaze
articles.summary: A major fire broke out at the Russian port of Ust-Luga in the Leningrad region following an overnight drone attack, Censor.net reports. According to ASTRA’s OSINT analysis, the northern part of "Novatek’s" production and processing complex for the fractionation and transshipment of stabilised gas condensate is burning.
articles.body: A major fire broke out at the Russian port of Ust-Luga in the Leningrad region following an overnight drone attack, Censor.net reports. According to ASTRA’s OSINT analysis, the northern part of "Novatek’s" production and processing complex for the fractionation and transshipment of stabilised gas condensate is burning. Following the drone attack that the Leningrad regional authorities reported last night, the northern production and processing cluster of the stabilised gas condensate (SGC) fractionation and transshipment complex of "NOVATEK-TRAS" LLC, "NATEK-TRA", is burning at Ust-Luga port. Several other fires are burning within the port. The first footage of the fire emerged overnight. At around six in the morning, the governor of the Leningrad region confirmed a "fire" in the Ust-Luga port area. He later reported that three people had been injured, while NASA satellites detected a large fire at Ust-Luga port.

articles.summary: BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 11. A landmine incident occurred near the village of Girmizi Bazar in the Khojavend District.
articles.body: BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 11. A landmine incident occurred near the village of Girmizi Bazar in the Khojavend District. According to ANAMA, on November 11, Iskandar Ismayilov, a resident of the Barda District born in 1984, was injured by an anti-tank mine while driving his tractor. As a result of the incident, Iskandar Ismayilov sustained injuries of varying severity. ANAMA, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and the General Prosecutor’s Office have urged citizens to observe safety rules, pay close attention to mine warning signs, avoid driving or walking into unfamiliar areas, and refrain from entering fenced-off areas.

Giorgi Sioridze: Georgian Dream has unmasked itself once again - they want to crown a constitutional coup with the formalization of a dictatorship
articles.summary: "We have heard a great deal of contradictions, a great deal of absurdity today once again, and 'Georgian Dream' has unmasked itself yet another time," stated Giorgi Sioridze, a representative of "Strong Georgia - Lelo," following the conclusion of the session at the Constitutional Court, where the plenum of judges is reviewing "Georgian Dream's" lawsuit on banning political parties.
articles.body: "We have heard a great deal of contradictions, a great deal of absurdity today once again, and 'Georgian Dream' has unmasked itself yet another time," stated Giorgi Sioridze, a representative of "Strong Georgia - Lelo," following the conclusion of the session at the Constitutional Court, where the plenum of judges is reviewing "Georgian Dream's" lawsuit on banning political parties. According to Sioridze, through the answers given to the judges' questions, "Georgian Dream" once again laid bare the absurdity of its lawsuit and showed the real purpose behind this process. "The judges had quite interesting questions for the representatives of 'Georgian Dream,' to which 'Georgian Dream' gave astonishing answers—answers that once again luminate [expose] this political force, once again reveal the absurdity of this lawsuit, and bring to light the real goal that this process has. It is a shameful page in modern history when a single political, authoritarian ruling force tries to eradicate the opposition, trying to commit violence against the will of the vast majority of society—according to their own official data, about 40% of voters, one million citizens—whom they are telling: formally you have the right to participate in elections, but no one you want to vote for will be there. There are so many contradictions, we have heard so much absurdity today again, and 'Georgian Dream' has unmasked itself once again. The constitutional coup that 'Georgian Dream' has been pursuing for years, which meant the complete subordination of the state apparatus, its subordination to a party vertical, which meant the adoption of regulations that would formally give them the opportunity through legalistic methods to establish a dictatorship—now they want to crown this with the banning of parties, the disappearance of the opposition from the political field, and the formalization of a dictatorship. At the same time, they have a second goal: turning their anti-Georgian, anti-national, anti-Western, and—most alarmingly—pro-Russian foreign policy into a constitutional obligation and rule. They also spoke about the 2008 war, as if they were standing guard over the dignity of Georgian servicemen. This is a statement by a political force whose one of the leaders, Ms. Tsulukiani, was telling us recently why Antsukhelidze is not at home and why Antsukhelidze died. In reality, they are trying to shift the responsibility of the occupying country onto the Georgian state, and at the same time they are trying to declare any dissenting opinion that might arise in the public space as sabotage if it criticizes 'Georgian Dream's' foreign policy," Sioridze stated.

articles.title: Gvaramia on lawsuit seeking to ban 5 opposition parties: The decision has been made; now, it’s just a matter of dressing it up
articles.summary: Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Coalition for Change, said the decision had already been made and that the ongoing proceedings were merely an attempt to “whitewash” it, following the conclusion of a Constitutional Court hearing. Gvaramia said the court had rejected a request to hold an evidentiary hearing, describing the decision as “absolutely unthinkable” and inconsistent with legal requirements.
articles.body: Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Coalition for Change, said the decision had already been made and that the ongoing proceedings were merely an attempt to “whitewash” it, following the conclusion of a Constitutional Court hearing. Gvaramia said the court had rejected a request to hold an evidentiary hearing, describing the decision as “absolutely unthinkable” and inconsistent with legal requirements. “What happened regarding the evidence is extremely problematic. I do not know how the court intends to get out of this situation. The entire stage of judicial examination has effectively been removed. This is absolutely unthinkable and does not comply with the requirements of the law,” Gvaramia said. He added that this was not the first time procedural fairness had worked against the opposition, claiming that the court had deprived the defendants of several procedural rights, including the opportunity to call witnesses and request evidence. “This really goes beyond everything. An entire stage has been removed altogether,” he said. Lelo - Strong Georgia had requested that the Constitutional Court hold an evidentiary hearing during proceedings on a lawsuit filed by Georgian Dream MPs seeking to ban five opposition parties. The motion was submitted by Levan Samushia, a representative of the respondent parties, and was supported by representatives of other opposition parties. The Constitutional Court's Plenum partially granted Lelo - Strong Georgia's motion to examine evidence during the hearing.

Serbian Ex-Minister Arrested for Suspected Abuse of Office
articles.summary: Former Economy Minister Rade Basta is suspected of abusing his office while running a Belgrade power utility company by approving unjustified donations to various sports associations.
articles.body: Former Serbian Economy Minister Rade Basta. Photo: Serbian Economy Ministry. Former Economy Minister Rade Basta was arrested on Tuesday on suspicion of defrauding public utility company Beogradske Elektrane (Belgrade Powerplants) of around 120,000 euros during his tenure as its director, the Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office in Belgrade confirmed. It is claimed that the money was improperly channeled to various sports clubs and associations while he headed Beogradske Elektrane from 2020 to 2022. Basta has not commented publicly on the allegations so far. Basta was Serbia’s Economy Minister in the government led by Aleksandar Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party from 2022 to 2023. He was dismissed after calling on the government to impose sanctions on Russia because of “its aggression against Ukraine”. He subsequently founded the European Way movement. He had been appointed minister as a member of United Serbia, a party that subsequently demanded his removal from all positions to which it had nominated him following his remarks on Russia. Basta recently applauded the Serbian Progressive Party’s defeat in last month’s parliamentary elections. He told Serbian Times that he has long believed that “the moment would come when citizens would no longer accept a policy of fear, pressure and control over institutions”. According to the Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office, the other suspects in the case against Basta include the executive director of Beogradske Elektrane and legal representatives of various sports clubs to which the money was allegedly channelled. The prosecutor’s office said Basta was charged with abuse of his official position while the Beogradske Elektrane director was charged with abuse of official position in aiding and abetting the offence. The other suspects were charged with money laundering. “The suspects will be held in custody for up to 48 hours, during which time they will be brought in for questioning,” the Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office said.

articles.title: US may pull $1.6B in funding for Kazakh mine backed by Trump sons
articles.summary: Two U.S. government-backed financial institutions — the Export-Import Bank of the United States (EXIM) and the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) — are not yet ready to approve $1.6 billion in financing for Cove Kaz Capital’s tungsten project in Kazakhstan. According to Bloomberg, which reported on the matter in an article highlighted by economist ...
articles.body: Two U.S. government-backed financial institutions — the Export-Import Bank of the United States (EXIM) and the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) — are not yet ready to approve $1.6 billion in financing for Cove Kaz Capital’s tungsten project in Kazakhstan. According to Bloomberg, which reported on the matter in an article highlighted by economist Arman Batayev , lenders have concerns about the project’s commercial prospects and geopolitical risks, including Kazakhstan’s proximity to China and Russia. The project has the backing of U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration, which is seeking to reduce American dependence on Chinese tungsten supplies. The metal is considered strategically important and is used in defense applications, including the production of missiles and artillery shells, as well as in various industrial technologies. The proposed financing package consists of two parts: $900 million from EXIM and $700 million from the DFC. Both institutions have issued letters of interest indicating potential support for the project. However, these documents represent preliminary expressions of interest and do not constitute binding financing commitments. A DFC representative told Bloomberg that the agency is not currently reviewing the proposed transaction. The Cove Kaz Capital project remains in the first of four stages of the DFC’s evaluation process. Meanwhile, EXIM’s letter of interest expired in August, and the company has requested an extension. The bank declined to comment. Cove Kaz Capital maintains that the U.S. government continues to support the project. Company Chairman Pini Althaus said a formal financing application would be submitted after the definitive feasibility study is completed in 2027. He added that the company does not currently need borrowed funds. Despite uncertainty surrounding U.S. government financing, Cove Kaz Capital is continuing preparations for a public listing. On Nov. 2, the company announced plans to list directly on a major U.S. stock exchange under the name Kaz Resources, targeting the first half of 2027. The announcement also disclosed a new $32 million capital commitment from an American investment vehicle. The funding, at $8 per share, implies an equity valuation of approximately $1.97 billion — a 76% increase over the company’s previous valuation. According to The Wall Street Journal, the investment vehicle is linked to Donald Trump’s sons, Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump . The brothers are expected to hold an indirect stake of less than 1% in the business. A representative for the brothers said they have no role in its management. The company has also denied their involvement in the execution of the Kazakhstan project. Kaz Resources expects to begin supplying tungsten to U.S. customers under long-term contracts once production gets underway, with initial output targeted for 2031. Kaz Resources’ main asset in Kazakhstan is its 70% stake in Severny Katpar LLP , the joint venture developing the Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty tungsten deposits in the Karaganda region. The remaining 30% is owned by Kazakhstan’s national mining company, Tau-Ken Samruk, a subsidiary of sovereign wealth fund Samruk-Kazyna. In May 2026, Cove Kaz Capital completed the acquisition of its controlling stake in the joint venture. The transaction was valued at $114.8 million. According to the company, the two deposits together could eventually account for approximately 15% of global tungsten mine production once the facilities reach their planned capacity. The company is currently conducting a definitive feasibility study for the project and expects to begin production in 2030. Kaz Resources had previously planned to enter the Nasdaq market through a merger with Hong Kong-based Skyline Builders Group. However, on Nov. 2, the companies announced that they had mutually terminated their business combination agreement. Cove Kaz Capital now intends to pursue a direct listing on a major U.S. stock exchange in the first half of 2027.

articles.title: Becirovic and Komsic discussed strengthening Cooperation between BiH and Turkey with Erdogan
articles.summary: The Chairman of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Denis Bećirović, and Presidency member Željko Komšić met in Antalya with the President of the Republic of Türkiye, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, on the sidelines of the Leaders’ Summit at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference.
articles.body: The Chairman of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Denis Bećirović, and Presidency member Željko Komšić met in Antalya with the President of the Republic of Türkiye, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, on the sidelines of the Leaders’ Summit at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference. During the meeting, the two sides discussed bilateral relations between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Türkiye, with a particular focus on enhancing political and economic cooperation. Bećirović and Komšić thanked Erdoğan for his hospitality and congratulated Türkiye on hosting the 31st UN Climate Change Conference, which brought together tens of thousands of participants from across the globe, the Presidency of BiH stated. According to the statement, the interlocutors reaffirmed their commitment to further strengthening and advancing cooperation between BiH and Türkiye—a relationship characterized by traditional friendship and a strong partnership. The importance of implementing joint projects and initiatives, as well as maintaining continuous political dialogue, was highlighted. The need to sustain and intensify meetings and the exchange of visits at the highest state level was also emphasized. The meeting was also attended by the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Türkiye, Hakan Fidan, the statement noted.

articles.title: Konakovic and Ginkel discuss BiH-US Partnership, Political Stability and Energy Security
articles.summary: The Minister of Foreign Affairs of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Elmedin Konaković, met on Tuesday with John Ginkel, Chargé d’Affaires at the United States Embassy in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The discussion covered the political and security situation, post-election processes, and the further development of cooperation between Bosnia and Herzegovina and the United States.
articles.body: The Minister of Foreign Affairs of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Elmedin Konaković, met on Tuesday with John Ginkel, Chargé d’Affaires at the United States Embassy in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The discussion covered the political and security situation, post-election processes, and the further development of cooperation between Bosnia and Herzegovina and the United States. The interlocutors exchanged views on the election results in both the United States and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Konaković emphasized the responsibility of political actors in BiH to form governments at all levels without unnecessary delay, thereby enabling institutions to focus on reforms and economic development. The Minister highlighted that the United States is one of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s key strategic partners and that its robust engagement remains of particular importance for the country’s peace and stability. He underscored the importance of consistent support for the Office of the High Representative (OHR) and the High Representative, whose role in implementing the Dayton Peace Agreement and safeguarding the constitutional order is crucial for the stability of Bosnia and Herzegovina – at least until all conditions of the “5+2 Agenda” are fully met. The discussion on further strengthening economic ties also addressed energy cooperation, with a specific focus on the “Southern Interconnection” project. Konaković highlighted the significance of this project for establishing an additional natural gas supply route, reducing energy dependency, and ensuring long-term security of supply for both citizens and the economy. He emphasized that cooperation with the U.S. in this area offers an opportunity to further strengthen the strategic partnership through concrete projects of long-term significance for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

articles.title: Komsic and Becirovic at COP31 Leaders Summit in Antalya
articles.summary: Željko Komšić, a member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, is attending the opening ceremony of the COP31 Leaders’ Summit in Antalya today, where he held discussions with the leaders of Austria and Montenegro, Alexander Van der Bellen and Jakov Milatović.
articles.body: Željko Komšić, a member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, is attending the opening ceremony of the COP31 Leaders’ Summit in Antalya today, where he held discussions with the leaders of Austria and Montenegro, Alexander Van der Bellen and Jakov Milatović. World leaders were welcomed at the ceremony by the President of Turkey, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, and the Secretary-General of the United Nations, António Guterres, the Presidency of BiH announced. A bilateral meeting between Komšić, the Chairman of the Presidency of BiH Denis Bećirović, and Erdoğan is also scheduled for later. This year’s summit focuses on strengthening international cooperation and translating global climate commitments into concrete actions and results. The goal is collective action in addressing climate change and its consequences.

articles.title: Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov officially files for a second term in 2027
articles.summary: Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov has submitted his documents to the Central Election Commission (CEC) to register as a candidate in the upcoming presidential election. The incumbent leader intends to seek a second term, Kaktus.media reported.
articles.body: Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov has submitted his documents to the Central Election Commission (CEC) to register as a candidate in the upcoming presidential election. The incumbent leader intends to seek a second term, Kaktus.media reported. He previously won the snap presidential election on Jan. 10, 2021, securing 79.2% of the vote. He officially assumed office on Jan. 28, 2021. Previously, the president was elected for a six-year term. However, following the adoption of a new Constitution in 2021, the presidential term was shortened to five years, with the possibility of serving two consecutive terms. To qualify as a presidential candidate, an individual must be a Kyrgyz citizen aged at least 35 and collect at least 30,000 supporting signatures. Candidates must also pay an electoral deposit of 1 million soms and submit a certificate confirming that they have passed the Kyrgyz language proficiency examination, known as the Kyrgyztest, at an above-average level. They must also provide documentation confirming that they do not hold citizenship of another country. In addition to Japarov, five other individuals have submitted their documents to the CEC: Aymen Kasenov , Azamat Esenbekov , Syimyk Japykeev , Akai Kydyrov , Iskhak Masaliev .

Millions join Spain’s first general strike in 14 years in protest at housing costs
articles.summary: Twenty-four-hour stoppage draws high participation weeks before election in which far right could gain power Millions of people across Spain have joined the country’s first general strike in 14 years, setting up picket lines to protest against soaring housing prices before an election in which the far right could be catapulted into power.
articles.body: Millions of people across Spain have joined the country’s first general strike in 14 years, setting up picket lines to protest against soaring housing prices before an election in which the far right could be catapulted into power. At the centre of Wednesday’s nationwide 24-hour stoppage, singularly called for by tenants’ associations and later backed by workers’ unions, is a pushback against Spain’s deepening housing crisis. Sandra Mora, of the Madrid Tenants’ Union, told the broadcaster RNE: “It’s extremely important to remind people that we, the workers – who are also renters or who also pay mortgages – are the ones with the power to halt production and bring the economy to a standstill.” While workers’ unions reported high participation in the strike across several sectors, including 90% in the automotive and port sectors and 82% in waste collection, they said participation was uneven across the country. The strongest support was reported in coastal regions, such as Catalonia and Andalucía, where the soaring cost of housing has been particularly acute. The Confederation of Tenants’ Association described the strike as a success, saying in a statement that by midday about 4 million people had taken part. Many schools and universities were reportedly closed or working at minimal capacity. In Madrid, the labour action added to a continuing teachers’ strike that began nearly a month ago to demand better working conditions. In Barcelona, workers set up roadblocks – some with burning tyres – as public transport came to a near-standstill. Pickets were in place soon after the strike began at midnight, blocking off entry to factories, markets and transport hubs. Key roads into Barcelona, including the AP-7 motorway, were blocked off in both directions. In Madrid, scuffles broke out between pickets and police near the country’s main wholesale market, while thousands of demonstrators poured into the city’s main boulevard, halting traffic temporarily. Government officials said more than 50 people had been arrested over minor incidents across the country. Bad weather loomed over plans for afternoon marches after Spain’s state meteorological agency issued 14 alerts for two storms that were expected to bring strong winds, heavy rain and rough seas. Tens of thousands of people still came together in more than 90 marches, pouring into plazas in Barcelona, Madrid and other cities. The marches in Cádiz, Seville, Córdoba and Huelva had to be cancelled amid forecasts of winds gusting up to 75mph (120km/h). The long-simmering frustration at soaring housing prices across Spain burst into public view in September after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the home in which she had lived for more than seven decades. As protests and encampments sprang up across Spain, it cast a spotlight on a market where properties have been increasingly used as tourist lets, speculative assets and short-term rentals, sending rents rising by 80% within a decade while the cost of homes climbed by 63%. Before Wednesday’s strike, the tenants’ union of Granada sought to highlight this link, descending on the city’s most touristy areas to vandalise about 300 lockboxes belonging to short-term rentals. “No to capitalists, no to rent-seekers, no to their accomplices,” the organisation wrote on social media, as they posted pictures of lockboxes that had been rendered unusable. Housing campaigners and unions have called on the government to do more to intervene in the market, with tenants’ unions demanding measures such as a crackdown on housing speculation, the elimination of tourist lets and strengthened protections for renters. While nominal wages for many across Spain had risen in recent years, Unai Sordo, the head of Spain’s biggest labour union, the Workers’ Commissions, said no amount of collective bargaining would be enough to address housing costs that had climbed by as much as 12% annually. “There is one issue that is fracturing the country, and that is the difficulty many people face in accessing housing,” he told the broadcaster Cadena Ser. Spain is holding a general election on 29 November. The snap vote was called by the Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez , after rightwing parties torpedoed emergency legislation aimed at tackling the housing crisis. Polls suggest the most likely outcome will be a rightwing coalition between the People’s party and the far-right, anti-immigration Vox party. While Sánchez has sought to focus the campaign on social issues, the discussion has shifted to questions over infrastructure after at least 69 people were killed in Spain’s second deadly high-speed rail disaster this year. This week Sánchez seized on the strike, whose official slogan is “Salaries. Housing. Prices”, as a way to recast the spotlight, posting a video in which he lauded developments such as the eight-hour work day and national health insurance and credited them to the labour movement and the right to strike. “It wasn’t easy, but they changed Spain,” Sánchez said. His position sharply contrasted with the discourse of parties on the right who, in the lead-up to the strike, dismissed it as an effort by unions to help Sánchez remain in office. This week the rightwing leader of the Madrid region, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, accused striking workers of “holding citizens hostage”. Ayuso, who this year faced questions over her administration’s decision to allegedly spend €6.3m (£5.4m) of public funds on a residential penthouse to use as a temporary office, added: “Everything is chaotic, everything is gridlocked.” While she acknowledged union activity was a constitutional right, she also took aim at what she described as the “mafia of union representatives” and said she had vented her frustrations to the leader of the People’s party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, who polls suggest will be the next prime minister. “I’ll confess something,” she told Spanish television. “I spoke to Feijóo and I told him: ‘Promise me this garbage will end.’”
